title: Symplectic lattice gauge theories in the Grid framework: domain wall fermions and continuum extrapolations
summary: We report the results of the first numerical lattice study using domain-wall fermions in the Sp(4) gauge theory coupled to two flavours of (Dirac) fermions, transforming in the fundamental representation of the gauge group. This theory plays a prominent role in the literature on extensions of the Standard Model with composite dynamics. It provides a short-distance completion for a class of composite Higgs models, or, alternatively, of dark matter models based on the strongly interacting massive particle paradigm. We adopt the Möbius formulation of domain-wall fermions (MDWF), implemented within the Grid software environment. We report the results of extensive tests of the algorithm implementation, and of the optimisation of the choices of algorithmic parameters appearing in the MDWF action. We then measure masses and decay constants of the lightest flavoured mesons in ensembles with moderately large fermion masses and several choices of lattice coupling, and perform an extrapolation to the continuum. We compare our results for the physical observables to published measurements obtained in the same field theory, but derived on the lattice by employing Wilson fermions. We demonstrate that, with the deployment of moderate computational resources, the MDWF formulation can yield order-of-magnitude gains in the approach to the continuum limit, in regions of physical parameter space relevant to phenomenological applications of this theory.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the first numerical lattice study using domain-wall fermions in Sp(4) gauge theory, which is significant for extending the Standard Model. It demonstrates that the MDWF formulation can achieve substantial gains in the approach to the continuum limit with moderate computational resources.
AI.motivation: To explore and validate the use of domain-wall fermions (MDWF) in the Sp(4) gauge theory as a means to extend the Standard Model, offering a short-distance completion for composite Higgs models or dark matter models, and to compare its effectiveness against Wilson fermions in lattice simulations.
AI.method: Conducted extensive tests and optimizations of algorithmic parameters for the MDWF action within the Grid software environment. Measured meson masses and decay constants on ensembles with varying fermion masses and lattice couplings, and performed an extrapolation to the continuum limit.
AI.result: Achieved order-of-magnitude gains in the approach to the continuum limit with the MDWF formulation compared to Wilson fermions, under conditions relevant for phenomenological applications, using only moderate computational resources.
AI.conclusion: The MDWF formulation is more efficient in approaching the continuum limit than Wilson fermions, making it a promising tool for further studies in the Sp(4) gauge theory and its applications in particle physics.

title: Numerical Investigations of Phase Transitions in Lattice Field Theories
comment: PhD Thesis, IISER Mohali (2026), based on arXiv:2307.13593, arXiv:2404.17504, arXiv:2508.05595, arXiv:2601.17436
summary: The study of phase transitions plays an important role in understanding qualitative changes in the behaviour of physical systems at criticality. Despite decades of progress, there is still a strong demand for high-precision numerical tools capable of resolving subtle critical phenomena. Motivated by this need, in this thesis, we present two complementary numerical investigations of phase transitions in lattice systems. The first uses GPU-accelerated higher-order tensor renormalization group (HOTRG) techniques to study the two-dimensional generalized XY model, characterizing its ferromagnetic, nematic, and paramagnetic phases and mapping their phase boundaries using thermodynamic observables in the thermodynamic limit. The second develops and benchmarks a configurational temperature estimator, constructed from gradients and Hessians of the Euclidean lattice action, in compact U(1) lattice gauge theories. On one hand, tensor network methods capture rich phase structures when truncation and finite-bond effects are adequately controlled. On the other hand, the configurational temperature estimator provides an independent, low-overhead means of validating thermal sampling across different algorithms and models, and can also be used as a runtime diagnostic to identify sampling pathologies before large-scale production runs.

AI.tldr: This thesis presents two numerical methods for studying phase transitions in lattice systems: GPU-accelerated HOTRG to study the 2D generalized XY model and a configurational temperature estimator for U(1) lattice gauge theories, aiming to provide high-precision tools for resolving critical phenomena.
AI.motivation: The motivation is driven by the need for high-precision numerical tools to understand subtle critical phenomena in physical systems at phase transitions, where existing methods may not be sufficient to resolve such subtleties.
AI.method: The first method employs GPU-accelerated higher-order tensor renormalization group (HOTRG) to investigate the 2D generalized XY model. The second method involves the development and benchmarking of a configurational temperature estimator, which is based on the gradients and Hessians of the Euclidean lattice action, specifically applied to compact U(1) lattice gauge theories.
AI.result: The HOTRG method successfully characterizes ferromagnetic, nematic, and paramagnetic phases and maps their boundaries using thermodynamic observables. The configurational temperature estimator provides a way to validate thermal sampling and can also diagnose sampling issues before large-scale simulations are carried out.
AI.conclusion: Both the HOTRG and the configurational temperature estimator offer complementary approaches to the study of phase transitions, with the former being powerful for capturing complex phase structures, and the latter providing a means for validation and diagnostics of thermal sampling, together enhancing the precision and reliability of phase transition studies.

title: Computability of GPDs near $x=\pmξ$ in Lattice QCD
summary: In lattice QCD computations of generalized parton distributions (GPDs), the large momentum expansion generally requires all hard scales, $2|x\pmξ|P^z$ and $2|1\pm x|P^z$, to be much larger than $Λ_{\rm QCD}$. We show that this condition can be relaxed for $2|x\pmξ|P^z$ at large $ξ$, making the important $x\sim\pmξ$ regions accessible to lattice calculations and considerably expanding the region of computability. Revisiting previous lattice results with complete one-loop matching, we obtain the expected partonic threshold behavior---GPDs continuous at $x=\pmξ$ but with discontinuous derivatives---which has not previously been observed on the lattice. We thus obtain, for the first time, important prediction for GPDs in the distribution-amplitude-like region, which smoothly connects the quark and antiquark PDF-like behaviors.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that the condition for large momentum expansion in GPDs calculations can be relaxed, allowing for a wider range of computations and revealing the expected partonic threshold behavior, which connects quark and antiquark PDF-like behaviors.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to expand the region of computability in lattice QCD computations of generalized parton distributions (GPDs) by relaxing the requirement on one of the hard scales, thereby making it possible to explore previously inaccessible regions and to observe the expected partonic threshold behavior.
AI.method: The authors revisit previous lattice results with complete one-loop matching, allowing them to relax the condition on 2|x±ξ|P^z at large ξ, which makes the x∼±ξ regions accessible to lattice calculations.
AI.result: By relaxing the condition, the authors are able to observe the expected partonic threshold behavior, where GPDs are continuous at x=±ξ but have discontinuous derivatives. This provides a connection between quark and antiquark PDF-like behaviors, an important prediction for GPDs in the distribution-amplitude-like region.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion is that by relaxing the large momentum condition, the study has expanded the computational reach for GPDs, enabling the observation of partonic threshold behavior, and providing new insights into the connection between quark and antiquark PDF-like behaviors.
